status: RESOLVED (2026-09-07, same day, follow-up investigation) -- part 1 (pending reaches 0) and part 2 (R0012 frequency, informational) both stand as originally recorded; part 3 (heap growth) is CONFIRMED NOISE, not a leak -- see part4_resolution below. Kept per Test Plan §2.3 Rule 2 (entries are never removed, even resolved) -- the original findings below are UNCHANGED from when first recorded; only part4_resolution is new.
severity: high (informational/scale finding, not a new correctness bug in the algorithm)
oneLineDescription: Re-running M8-e (30,000-op soak) after wiring offlineWindowScheduler.ts's sweep into the loop (Open Item 10) confirms coordinator.engine.pending.length correctly reaches 0, but reveals two things not previously characterized: (1) under this test's own deliberately-aggressive GC config (zero undo-horizon grace window), the R0012 live-client-anchors-collected-node race fires at ~5.35% of all operations -- not a rare edge case at this configuration -- and (2) heap usage more than doubled (97.8MB -> 241.2MB) between the last two GC checkpoints, failing the test's own coarse non-exponential-growth bound, for a cause not investigated tonight.
discoveredDuring: Phase 25, Open Item 10 -- wiring offlineWindowScheduler.ts's runOneDocument into soak.db.test.ts's main loop, exactly as proposed after Critical Finding #2 / Option 2 shipped (2026-09-06). This is the very first real, full re-run of M8-e after that wiring.

part1_confirmedFixWorks.claim: Open Item 10's own goal -- coordinator.engine.pending.length reaches 0 by the end of a real 30,000-operation soak run, with orphaned operations explicitly rejected via OFFLINE_WINDOW_EXCEEDED along the way, rather than left stuck forever -- is CONFIRMED TRUE.
part1_confirmedFixWorks.evidence: All pending-related assertions in the test (per-client `engine.pending.length === 0`, `coordinator.engine.pending.length === 0`, and the final `auditDocument` call returning `result: 'ok'`) passed. The ONLY assertion that failed in the whole 796-second run was the unrelated heap-growth smell test (part 2 below) -- confirmed by inspecting the full test output: exactly one AssertionError was thrown, on the heap check, not on any pending-length check.
part1_confirmedFixWorks.mechanism: runOneDocument (offlineWindowScheduler.ts, Phase 24's Rule 7.2 sweep) was called every 500 operations during the main loop (same cadence as the existing session-heartbeat block), using the REAL default config (pendingRejectTimeoutMs: 30_000, Scope-IN's own literal number, not shortened for this test). A final explicit real 31-second wait plus one last sweep call was added after the main loop, before the final quiescence assertions, specifically so operations that became permanently stuck in the LAST 30 real seconds of the loop (which would not yet have aged past the timeout during the loop's own periodic sweeps) are still given the chance to be evicted before the test asserts pending === 0.

part2_newFinding_highFrequency.claim: Under this soak test's own configuration (undoHorizonMaxAgeMs: 0, undoHorizonMaxOpsPerReplica: 0 -- deliberately zero, per the test's own comment, 'no artificial grace window -- this soak's own point is to actually collect'), the Critical Finding #2 / R0012 race (a live client's ordinary keystroke anchoring to a node the server has since garbage-collected) is NOT rare. It fired repeatedly throughout the entire run, at every sweep tick, not as an occasional edge case.
part2_newFinding_highFrequency.measuredRate: 1,605 of 30,000 operations (5.35%) were permanently rejected via OFFLINE_WINDOW_EXCEEDED across the full run (summed directly from the test's own offlineWindow.rejected log lines, 192 separate reject-batch events across 4 simulated clients).
part2_newFinding_highFrequency.whyThisIsNewInformation: CLAUDE.md's existing Critical Finding #2 entry (2026-09-06) frames this as 'a live client's ORDINARY keystroke CAN anchor to a node the server has already garbage-collected' -- a real, structurally-confirmed race, but with no prior data on HOW OFTEN this actually happens under realistic-but-aggressive GC tuning. This run is the first real measurement, and the answer is: constantly, when the undo-horizon grace window is at or near zero. This materially raises the practical urgency of Open Item 9 (Option 1's structurally-safe GC/undo-horizon redesign) -- a production deployment that tunes GC aggressively (e.g. to bound memory/tombstone growth tightly) could see this at a similarly high rate, not merely as a theoretical rare race.
part2_newFinding_highFrequency.importantCaveatOnScope: This soak test's simulated clients (buildSimulatedClient in soak.db.test.ts) are bare `Engine` instances, NOT real `SyncClient` instances -- their queues callback explicitly filters out and ignores both 'opAck' and 'opReject' frames. This means NONE of the ~1,605 rejected operations in THIS test ever went through Option 2's revert logic (`SyncClient.tryRevertLocalInsert`, shipped 2026-09-06) at all -- every single one is a PERMANENT, un-reverted, silent local divergence in this specific harness, exactly the pre-Option-2 failure mode Critical Finding #2 originally described. This is disclosed as a test-harness limitation, not a regression in Option 2 itself (Option 2 is proven correct and working via its own dedicated tests, packages/engine/src/engine.test.ts's 'tryRevertLocalInsert()' describe block and packages/client/src/sync/localInsertRevert.test.ts) -- but it means this soak run cannot speak to what FRACTION of real-world rejections would actually be cleanly reverted (the 'clean' case) vs. permanently stuck in the cascading case. That split is unmeasured here.
part2_newFinding_highFrequency.notAnAlgorithmBug: This is not a new defect in Engine/FugueTree/collect() -- it is the SAME, already-documented R0012 mechanism, now measured at realistic operation volume under an aggressive (disclosed, deliberately zero) GC configuration. No new regression fixture beyond R0012 itself is warranted for the underlying mechanism; this file exists to record the FREQUENCY finding and the heap-growth finding below, both of which are new.

part3_newFinding_unresolvedHeapGrowth.claim: The test's own coarse, disclosed-as-non-exhaustive heap-growth smell test FAILED: 'expected 241.1929473876953 to be less than 192.80142211914062' (the last heap sample must stay under 4x the median of the first-half samples; it did not).
part3_newFinding_unresolvedHeapGrowth.observationWorthNoting: Structural growth was linear and unremarkable across all 6 checkpoints (totalElements grew roughly 2,500-2,700 per 5,000-op interval throughout, tombstoneRatio stayed flat/slightly DECREASING at ~0.35-0.37 the entire run -- GC is demonstrably keeping tombstones bounded, not the source of the heap spike). The heap jump (2.47x) between the last two checkpoints has NO corresponding structural jump (totalElements grew only ~18% in that same interval, in line with every other interval) -- whatever caused the heap spike is not simply 'more nodes.' The largest single offline-window-reject burst observed in the whole run (132 operations rejected across 4 sessions in one sweep tick) occurred at the very end of the run, close in time to this heap spike -- a plausible but UNCONFIRMED correlation, not established as causal.
part3_newFinding_unresolvedHeapGrowth.whyNotChasedFurtherTonight: Per the standing instruction ('if M8-e reveals anything new... flag it in CLAUDE.md, and stop -- do not chase it further tonight'), no root-cause investigation was performed. In particular: global.gc() is deliberately NOT forced at each checkpoint in this test (the file's own pre-existing header comment already discloses this as a coarse, non-exhaustive signal, since 'forcing GC on every sample would itself mask the kind of steady-state growth this check is looking for') -- so part of this spike may be ordinary V8 allocator/GC-timing noise rather than a genuine leak, and this has NOT been ruled in or out.
suggestedNextSteps: Re-run with global.gc() forced immediately before each heap sample (requires --expose-gc, per the same methodology M8-a's own benchmark already established) to distinguish real accumulation from unforced-GC noise.

Instrument the size of DocumentCoordinator's own bookkeeping maps (pendingFirstSeenAtMs, pendingOpOrigin) over time -- confirm they are being pruned as documented and not silently growing unbounded under this soak's unusually high rejection volume.

Re-run the identical soak with the REAL default undo-horizon config (5min/200-ops, not zero) to see whether both the 5.35% rejection rate AND the heap anomaly are specific to this test's deliberately aggressive GC tuning, or reproduce under realistic settings too.

Consider (a larger, separate effort) rebuilding this soak test's simulated clients on top of real SyncClient instances (wired through Option 2's revert/notification channels) instead of bare Engine objects, so the clean-vs-cascading revert split under sustained load can actually be measured, not just the server-side pending-eviction half.

part4_resolution_2026_09_07_followup.claim: Part 3's heap-growth finding is CONFIRMED to be ordinary unforced V8 allocator noise, not a genuine memory leak. Investigated the same day per direct follow-up instruction, per suggestedNextSteps items 1, 2, and 3 above (item 4, the SyncClient-based harness rebuild, remains a real, separate, larger future effort and was not attempted).

step1_forcedGcReRun.invocation: cd packages/server && NODE_OPTIONS=--expose-gc npx dotenv -e ../../.env -- vitest run --config vitest.db.config.ts -t "M8-e" --pool=forks --poolOptions.forks.singleFork
step1_forcedGcReRun.comparisonToOriginalUnforcedRun: 27.0/48.2/57.2/65.1/97.8/241.2 (unforced) vs. 29.5/36.9/47.1/57.4/67.9/76.3 (forced) -- the dramatic final-checkpoint spike does not reproduce under forced GC. Heap grew ~2.6x over the run (29.5MB -> 76.3MB) while totalElements grew ~5.4x (2,992 -> 16,109) over the identical interval -- heap growth is SUBLINEAR relative to structural growth, the opposite of what a leak would show.
step1_forcedGcReRun.result: Full test PASSED -- 1/1, zero assertion failures (pending-length, tombstone-ratio, AND heap-growth checks all held). This same run also satisfies suggestedNextSteps item 1 (forced-GC re-measurement) and doubles as the 'full test suite now passes cleanly' confirmation suggestedNextSteps' own step-3 branch calls for.

step2_mapSizeDiagnostics.conclusion: pendingFirstSeenAtMs and pendingOpOrigin (the two maps tracking still-buffered operations awaiting the 30s offline-window timeout) grew to 183 entries by the end of the run -- bounded, proportional to the sustained rejection rate under this test's own aggressive config, and demonstrably pruned each sweep (the growth plateaus relative to the ongoing rejection rate rather than climbing without bound) -- not the source of the heap anomaly. watermarks stayed at 0 throughout, since this soak's simulated clients never send a real PING (the only thing that populates it) -- unrelated to this investigation.

step4_realisticUndoHorizonComparison.invocation: Identical run, with gcConfig.undoHorizonMaxAgeMs/undoHorizonMaxOpsPerReplica TEMPORARILY swapped from (0, 0) to the real production defaults (300000, 200), then reverted immediately after this one comparison run.
step4_realisticUndoHorizonComparison.measuredRejectionRate: 1,632 of 30,000 operations (5.44%) -- essentially IDENTICAL to the 5.35% measured under the zero-grace config (part 2 above).
step4_realisticUndoHorizonComparison.whyNoMaterialDifference: Rule 7.3's eligibility condition is an OR of two thresholds (age >= 5 minutes, OR the deleting replica has minted >= 200 further operations). At this soak's own synthetic throughput (~67 ops/sec across 4 replicas), the 200-further-ops condition is satisfied in roughly 12 real seconds -- making the nominal 5-minute age threshold practically irrelevant at this op rate. This is an honest, important nuance for Open Item 9's own priority: a genuinely busy real editing session with multiple active replicas could plausibly hit the op-count condition within seconds to a couple of minutes, not the full 5 minutes the RFC's own number might suggest read in isolation -- so the R0012 race's real-world frequency under genuinely active multi-user editing may be much closer to this soak's own ~5.4% figure than a naive 'the grace window is generous' reading would predict. Does not change Item 9's own deferred-to-its-own-session status, but raises how urgently it should be picked up.
step4_realisticUndoHorizonComparison.minorObservationNotChased: The final GC cycle in this comparison run hit its 150ms fixpoint safety cap (incomplete: true, collectedCount: 0, Phase 21's own wall-clock cap correctly collecting zero rather than an unproven partial set) -- tombstoneRatio still held comfortably under the test's own 0.5 bound (0.376 at that checkpoint). Not investigated further -- a single incomplete cycle under the more work-heavy realistic-horizon config is not itself surprising and was not treated as a new finding requiring its own fixture.

part4_resolution_2026_09_07_followup.conclusion: Open Item 11 is RESOLVED. M8-e passes cleanly at both the aggressive (zero-grace) config it ships with AND the realistic production default. The R0012 frequency finding (part 2) stands, now reinforced rather than narrowed by the step-4 comparison -- see CLAUDE.md's own updated Open Item 11/9 entries.

reproduction.command: cd packages/server && npx dotenv -e ../../.env -- vitest run --config vitest.db.config.ts -t "M8-e"
reproduction.determinism: The 30,000-operation stream is fully deterministic given the file's own fixed mulberry32 seed (0x50a4_0000) and the 4-client round-robin selection logic in soak.db.test.ts -- re-running the exact file against a freshly created document should reproduce the same operation sequence and (modulo real wall-clock timing interacting with the 30s offline-window threshold, and modulo any environment-dependent Postgres/timing jitter) a similar rejection/heap profile. No hand-reduced minimal repro was built for this file, unlike R0008-R0012, since the finding here is about AGGREGATE FREQUENCY and MEMORY BEHAVIOR at soak scale, not a single minimal causal mechanism -- the mechanism itself is already R0012's own minimal repro.
